planting.note: Sow seed outdoors in fall so winter moisture and cold naturally soften the hard legume seed coat, or nick/scarify stored seed before a spring sowing; established plants resent transplanting because of their deep taproot.

directions: French grass is a tall, deep-rooted legume of calcareous bluff prairies and prairie-woodland margins, most familiar in the Midwest along the Missouri River Loess Hills where it grows with little bluestem and prairie dropseed on steep, wind-deposited silt slopes. Clover-scented spikes of small violet-purple, pea-shaped flowers rise above coarse, three-parted leaves in early to midsummer and are heavily worked by bumblebees and leafcutter bees. Its long taproot and nitrogen-fixing nodules let it persist on thin, well-drained bluff soils that bake dry in summer, so once established it needs no irrigation or fertilizer. Site it where it can be left undisturbed, since mature plants decline quickly if dug or moved.

planting.note: Scatter seed on the surface of bare, exposed sand in fall or do a short cold-moist stratification before spring sowing, since seed needs light and open ground to germinate and resents being buried; this species is historically associated with periodic fire or disturbance that keeps sand savannas open.

directions: Hoary frostweed is a low, gray-hairy subshrub of black-oak sand savannas and sand prairies across the Upper Midwest, growing in the same open, droughty sand that supports wild lupine and sand-ecotype little bluestem. Each short-lived, bright yellow five-petaled flower opens for only a few morning hours before dropping its petals, and later in the season the plant switches to small, closed cleistogamous flowers that self-pollinate without ever opening. Its taproot and compact, woody-based habit let it thrive in bare, loose sand where taller prairie plants struggle, making it a useful low front-of-border accent in a sand-garden or savanna-restoration planting. Keep it on lean, fast-draining sandy soil in full sun, since rich garden soil or excess moisture encourages floppy growth and rot.
